belief: I must hide my money problems.
origins: Many of us learned that money is private and that trouble should be kept inside the family. Fear of judgment, embarrassment about status, or a parent who always “kept up appearances” can teach us to hide. Hiding can start small, such as not mentioning a bill, and grow into secrecy from a spouse, friends, or church. The cost is isolation and a problem that has no helpers.
teaches: Scripture says that plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed. We are told to bear one another’s burdens and that two are better than one, because if one falls, the other can lift him up. James encourages us to confess to one another and pray for one another. None of this means we must tell everyone everything. It means we should not carry heavy things entirely alone, and that wise, safe people are part of God’s help.
self_statements: If anyone knew, I would be humiliated.
I have to look like I have everything under control.
It is better to say nothing.
People would think less of me.
errors: Predicting that others will judge or reject me.
Assuming I know what people would think.
Imagining that being found out would be a disaster.
Insisting that I must handle money problems alone.
questions: What am I afraid will happen if one safe person knows?
What has hiding cost me so far, in peace, sleep, and closeness?
Who has been honest with me about a hard time, and what did I think of them?
Who is a safe, wise person I could tell first?
What is the difference between privacy and secrecy?
What is the smallest honest step I could take this week?
truth: Privacy can be healthy, but secrecy about a heavy problem keeps me alone with it. God provides counselors, friends, family, and advisers. I can choose a safe person, share honestly, and let help in.
hw_truths: I do not have to carry this alone.
Safe people can carry part of the weight.
Honesty is not the same as telling everyone.
I can choose who to tell and when.
log: Each week, write down one honest step you took about money, who you told, and how it felt afterward.
actions: Pick someone trustworthy, discreet, and kind, such as a spouse, pastor, counselor, or friend.
Write what you want to say.
Draft two or three sentences that tell the truth simply.
Share it, ask for support or ideas, and notice how they respond.
Contact a nonprofit credit counselor, financial advisor, or church benevolence team if you need practical guidance.
prayer: Lord, You see what I have been hiding. Give me courage to be honest, and lead me to wise, safe people. Take the shame out of asking for help and let me not carry this alone. Amen.
hw_questions: Who is a safe person I could tell?
What am I afraid will happen?
What would I say to a friend in my place?
What is one honest step this week?
name_example: Sarah can write: “Plans succeed with wise counsel, so I can choose a safe person and tell the truth.”
